title: Golden Men of Jazz with Lionel Hampton, and teaching at school
summary: Mance works with Hampton's all-star group, news of Hampton's strokes, and his part-time teaching job.

bands.name: Lionel Hampton and the Golden Men of Jazz

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans

blocks.x: And then I’ve been working with another group called Lionel Hampton and the Golden Men of Jazz, which is an eight piece all star group. It changes from time to time but usually it’s Al Grey on trombone, Clark Terry and Harry “Sweets” Edison on trumpets, James Moody usually on tenor saxophone, Grady Tate usually on drums, and Milt Hinton or Jimmy Woode on bass. You know and that’s you say “Golden Men” because we’re all over 60. I think that’s the criteria for being a member of this group. But they do mostly all the jazz festivals in the summer. We were canceled this year because Lionel had another mild stroke just before we were supposed to leave. He’s okay now, he’s out of the hospital and but he’s a tough old man. He’s 87 years old and that was his second mild stroke since March and the third in the last three years. And he’s doing two things, you © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

know, he’s still got his big band going. The 29th of this month he’s going to do a gig with his big band. I said, oh, boy, I hope he doesn’t have another one, because we’re supposed to do some things in September. We’re going to a big jazz program at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles and they also are going to honor him again at the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C. And then other than that, well when school starts I’m a part time teacher. Whenever I’m there I teach. Because the faculty is made up of working jazz musicians and it’s what they want. It’s what most of the schools around here have. And so it’s even in our contract if we have to take off for a tour or a job or something, we are free to do so, just provide a substitute, which is very easy. Usually we’re able to get somebody in-house to do it. But we can get someone from outside. And I like that. I’ve been doing it for six years. I teach a blues class. You know, and it’s a lot of fun. First I declined, I said no I’m not a teacher, I’m a college dropout you know, I said I don’t have the credentials. They said “good, we don’t want teachers, we want performers. See because we don’t want to turn out more teachers, we want to turn out performers.” So most of the classes are performing, you know, very little textbook work you know, in fact there are hardly any, the only textbook they have is this so-called, I know you’re familiar with it, Mike, the “Real Book.” And we have to explain to them that to just use this as a guide, because there are many, many wrong changes. But it’s the best thing for them to go on, really, so it provides a guide. Anyway, that’s the textbook.
